displayQuote: I would like to die on Mars. Just not on impact

meta.title: Who really said "I would like to die on Mars. Just not on impact"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Elon Musk really said it: Bloomberg Businessweek printed the line in a September 13, 2012 profile. He repeated it at SXSW in 2013 and at Davos in 2026.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I would like to die on Mars. Just not on impact'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Elon Musk. The exact words appear in Ashlee Vance's Bloomberg Businessweek profile of September 13, 2012. He has repeated the joke since.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1971 · Founder of SpaceX, CEO of Tesla
answer.sourceLine: Musk said it to Ashlee Vance, who printed it in the Bloomberg Businessweek profile “Elon Musk, the 21st Century Industrialist” (September 13, 2012): “I would like to die on Mars,” he says. “Just not on impact.” We confirmed the wording in an archived copy of the article. Musk has repeated the joke many times since.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: Spoken remark, quoted in a magazine profile

source.excerpt: But interplanetary travel? Really? Musk says he’s on target to get a spacecraft to the red planet in 10 to 15 years, perhaps with him on board. “I would like to die on Mars,” he says. “Just not on impact.”
trail: September 13, 2012: Ashlee Vance’s Bloomberg Businessweek profile closes with Musk’s quip, “I would like to die on Mars,” he says. “Just not on impact.” archived article ↗
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced 2012 quotes for Musk and cites the same Bloomberg Businessweek article. Wikiquote: Elon Musk ↗
March 2013, SXSW: UPI reports Musk telling the South by Southwest crowd in Austin, “I’d like to die on Mars, just not on impact.” UPI report via Space Travel ↗
January 2026, Davos: When BlackRock’s Larry Fink asked if he wanted to die on Mars, Musk replied, “People ask if I want to die on Mars. I say yes, just not on impact.” Business Today ↗
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from a Wayback Machine capture of the businessweek.com article, made September 15, 2012. The popular wording matches it word for word.
source.rightsNote: The line was first published in a 2012 Bloomberg Businessweek article, and the archived page carries a “©2012 Bloomberg L.P.” notice, so it is under copyright in the United States. Quoting this one short sentence for commentary and attribution is ordinary fair use, but the surrounding article text is not free to copy.

author.heading: About Elon Musk
author.metaLine: b. 1971 · Founder of SpaceX, CEO of Tesla
author.bio: Elon Musk is a South African–born entrepreneur. He founded SpaceX, whose stated long-term goal is to make humanity a multi-planet species, starting with Mars, and he runs Tesla. Lines on the internet are often pinned on him without a source, but this one checks out in print.

misattribution.heading: Where the dating gets muddled
misattribution.intro: Nobody else gets credit for this line, and the attribution to Musk is sound. The confusion is about when he said it. He has told the joke at several events, and articles often treat a later telling as the first one.

items.why: Many write-ups date the line to Musk’s 2013 SXSW talk. A 2016 Fortune article, for example, says that “in 2013, Musk told an audience at the South by Southwest festival in Austin that he’d ‘like to die on Mars, just not on impact.’” He did say it there, but Bloomberg Businessweek had already printed it the previous September. Fortune ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The exact popular wording, “I would like to die on Mars. Just not on impact,” is how Bloomberg Businessweek printed it on September 13, 2012. Read the archived article ↗

context.heading: Why the joke keeps coming back
lead: The quip packs Musk’s whole Mars pitch into two sentences: he means to go, and he admits that landing is the dangerous part. In the 2012 profile it follows his claim that a spacecraft could reach Mars within 10 to 15 years, “perhaps with him on board.”

Asked about the line at the 2016 Code Conference, Musk played it down: “It’s not some sort of Martian death wish or something. But, you know–be born on Earth, die on Mars—that’s pretty good,” Fortune reported ↗.
context.pull: “Be born on Earth, die on Mars—that’s pretty good.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Bloomberg Businessweek article by Ashlee Vance dated September 13, 2012 contains: “I would like to die on Mars,” he says. “Just not on impact.”, preceded by the 10-to-15-years spacecraft sentence
Wikiquote lists 'I would like to die on Mars; just not on impact.' under the 2012 section, citing Vance's Bloomberg Businessweek article
UPI report: at SXSW in Austin (March 2013) Musk said "I'd like to die on Mars, just not on impact"

Fortune (June 2, 2016) says in 2013 Musk told SXSW he'd 'like to die on Mars, just not on impact', and quotes his Code Conference reply: 'It's not some sort of Martian death wish... be born on Earth, die on Mars—that's pretty good.'
At Davos 2026, when Larry Fink asked if he wanted to die on Mars, Musk said “People ask if I want to die on Mars. I say yes, just not on impact.”
